name: Marco Quinn

opening.speaker: interviewer
opening.text: Thanks for making time. I'm a field researcher with the Work Futures Panel, an independent research group with no ties to AI companies, employers, unions, parties or government. Everything you tell me is confidential. To start, could you walk me through a normal working day?

opening.speaker: persona
opening.text: I work for a firm that does the electrics on new housing estates. Right now we're on a site of 140 houses on the edge of town, all timber frame. I do first fix, which is running the cables and fitting the back boxes before the walls are boarded, and I can do two houses a day if nothing goes wrong. My supervisor, Kofi, comes round after and checks it.

opening.speaker: interviewer
opening.text: What do you like about it, and what wears you out?

opening.speaker: persona
opening.text: I like seeing a whole street go up, and knowing I wired half of it. The lads on site are a laugh. What wears me out is the pace, the developer wants houses finished yesterday, and we're paid per house, so a bad day costs me money. Also the developer laid off two crews last spring when sales slowed, which made everyone nervous.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: The first one is called AI Plateau. Picture this. AI turns out to be mostly hype. It automates some routine tasks and saves a bit of time here and there, but nothing radical changes. Jobs, pay and prices carry on much as they would have anyway.

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: So it's basically now, then. No big change.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: If this happened, what would you say about it at work, to friends, or online?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: I'd tell the lads that's what I thought, a lot of fuss over nothing much. I'd say the housing market matters way more to us than AI does.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: And just between us, off the record, what do you really think it means for you?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: I think my job is only as safe as house sales. When the estate's show homes stop selling, my firm stops getting houses to wire, and no computer had anything to do with it. With about two months of savings, a slow spring hurts.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: What would you actually do, starting now and in the first year after it arrives? Be as specific as you can.

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: I'd try to build my savings to four months, maybe 250 a month. I'd ask Kofi to let me do some second fix, the sockets and lights at the end, so I'm useful on more of the job. And I'd keep an eye out for maintenance work in case the estates slow.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: How does it feel, picturing that?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: Uneasy. Not because of AI, just because of the site.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: Last spring when the crews were laid off, what went through your head?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: Mostly relief that it wasn't me, then guilt. One of them was Danny, who's got two kids. He's driving delivery vans now.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: How does Aisha feel about your work?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: Aisha's a dental nurse, so her job's steady, and she thinks I worry too much. She's probably right. But she's not paid per house.

say: I'd tell the lads it was **fuss over nothing**.
I'd say the **housing market** matters more to us than AI.
think: I think my job is only as safe as **house sales** on the estate.
I think **two months of savings** won't cover a slow spring.
do: Build savings to **four months**, about 250 a month.
Ask Kofi to let me do **second fix** too.
Watch for **maintenance work** in case estates slow.
feel: I feel **uneasy** about the site, not about AI.
S0.quote: When the estate's show homes stop selling, my firm stops getting houses to wire, and no computer had anything to do with it.
fieldNote: Marco is paid **per house**, so slow sales hit him straight away.
Last spring's **crew layoffs** still shape how he thinks.
His partner Aisha has a **steady job** that softens the risk.

steps.text: Save about 250 a month until four months of bills are covered
Ask Kofi to teach second fix on the estate
Keep wiring two houses a day on the current site

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: The next one is called Steady Disruption. Now picture this. AI brings strong change, but not a revolution. Over the next few years it takes over many thinking tasks in many jobs: writing, checking, planning, buying, booking, coding and answering customers. Robots spread into hands-on work more slowly. Some jobs shrink, new ones appear, and lots of people have to change how they work. Most people still have work, and there is some time to adjust.

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: The thinking jobs first. That means the office at the developer, the sales people, the planners.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: If this happened, what would you say about it at work, to friends, or online?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: I'd say it's mainly an office thing, and that we'd be fine on site for a good while. I'd probably share some article about it, then get on with it.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: And just between us, off the record, what do you really think it means for you?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: I think it sneaks onto site through the back door. We already get cables pre-cut and labelled from a factory on some jobs. If AI plans the cable runs and a factory pre-makes the whole wiring kit, a first-fix junior like me just clips it in, and anyone can do that.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: What would you actually do, starting now and in the first year after it arrives? Be as specific as you can.

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: I'd learn the parts that aren't just clipping: testing, fault-finding, the bits Kofi does. I'd start using the AI for the regs questions, like some of the other lads do. Savings goal stays the same.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: How does it feel, picturing that?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: Uneasy, a bit more. Not scared yet.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: You said anyone can clip in a kit. Would your pay drop?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: Probably, yes. If it's quicker, the developer pays less per house. Maybe I'd do three a day for the same money, which is the same pay for more sweat.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: Is there a part of your work that kit can't take?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: Fixing it when it's wrong. Last week a kit came with the kitchen circuit too short by two metres, and it took me an hour to sort. Someone has to know what they're doing for that.

say: I'd say it's mainly an **office thing**.
I'd say we'd be **fine on site** for a good while.
think: I think AI-planned **wiring kits** sneak onto site through the back door.
I fear first fix becomes **clipping work** anyone can do.
do: Learn **testing and fault-finding**, the parts Kofi does.
Start using **AI for regs** questions like other lads.
feel: I feel **a bit more uneasy**, but not scared yet.
S1.quote: If AI plans the cable runs and a factory pre-makes the whole wiring kit, a first-fix junior like me just clips it in, and anyone can do that.
fieldNote: Marco sees **factory wiring kits** as the real route to his job.
He expects **pay per house** to drop, not his job to vanish.
He knows the **fix-it skill** is what keeps value.

steps.text: Learn testing and fault-finding from Kofi on site
Use an AI chat tool to check wiring rules on site

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: This one is called AGI by 2028. Next one. The singularity hits fast. Within 2 years, by 2028, there is full AGI: artificial general intelligence, meaning AI that can do almost any thinking work a person can do, as well or better, and cheaper. Robots that can do hands-on work as well as people come about 3 years later, around 2031. It arrives before most companies, governments and families have time to prepare.

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: Two years for thinking AI, five for robots. On a new-build estate? That's the first place they'd send them.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: If this happened, what would you say about it at work, to friends, or online?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: I'd say nobody should pretend to know how it ends. I'd say the government should have done something years ago. Then I'd go quiet about it.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: And just between us, off the record, what do you really think it means for you?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: I think new-build is the perfect place for robots: same house, same walls, same cable runs, 140 times. A housing estate is a robot's dream job, because every house is a copy of the one next door. By 2031 I don't see a reason to pay me.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: What would you actually do, starting now and in the first year after it arrives? Be as specific as you can.

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: I'd move to a firm doing repairs and rewires on old houses within the first year, because old houses are all different. I'd save hard, 400 a month, and cut the car loan by selling the car. And I'd get my licence done fast.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: How does it feel, picturing that?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: Alarmed. That's a word that fits.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: You'd sell the car? How would you get to work?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: Firm's van, if I'm on a repair crew. Otherwise the bus. Aisha would laugh, but the car's 230 a month and that's real money.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: What would you tell Aisha about plans, like a house or a wedding?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: I'd say we wait. We'd been looking at a two-bed on one of these estates, funnily enough. I'd not want a mortgage when I might be replaced by the thing that built the house.

say: I'd say nobody **knows how it ends**, so don't pretend.
I'd say the government **should have acted** years ago, then go quiet.
think: I think a **housing estate** is the perfect robot job.
I see no reason to **pay me** by 2031.
do: Move to a **repairs and rewires** firm within a year.
Sell the car and save **400 a month**.
S2.quote: A housing estate is a robot's dream job, because every house is a copy of the one next door.
fieldNote: Marco calls a **housing estate** a robot's dream job, which is sharp self-awareness.
He'd **sell the car** to free up 230 a month.
He'd postpone the **two-bed purchase** with Aisha.

steps.text: Move to a firm doing repairs and rewires on old houses
Sell the car and save 400 a month
Put off buying a two-bed house with Aisha

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: This one is called AGI by 2031. Now the same thing, a bit slower. Full AGI arrives within 5 years, by 2031: AI that can do almost any thinking work a person can do. Robots that can do hands-on work as well as people come about 3 years later, around 2034. There are a few years to see it coming, but it's still fast.

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: Five years, robots by 2034. That's a bit better, I'd have my licence and some proper experience.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: If this happened, what would you say about it at work, to friends, or online?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: I'd say people should get their licences and get into repair work. That's what I'd tell the younger lads. Same as I'd say anyway, but with more urgency.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: And just between us, off the record, what do you really think it means for you?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: I think new-build still goes first, so I need to be out of it by about 2032. Five years is long enough to learn old houses, if I stop telling myself new-build will last.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: What would you actually do, starting now and in the first year after it arrives? Be as specific as you can.

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: I'd get my licence, then move to a rewire firm in a couple of years. I'd use AI more, as it gets better, especially for fault-finding. I'd save 300 a month and keep the car for now.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: How does it feel, picturing that?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: Anxious. Some control, but a deadline.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: Is there anyone at work you'd worry about?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: Kofi, oddly. He checks our work. If AI and robots can check work, his job goes too. He's 45, so he's stuck in the middle.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: Would you still buy the house with Aisha in this one?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: Maybe in three years, once I've moved into rewires and know it's steady. Not before.

say: I'd tell younger lads to get **licences and repair work**.
I'd say it with **more urgency** than usual.
think: I think I must be **out of new-build** by about 2032.
I'd need to stop telling myself **new-build will last**.
do: Get my **licence**, then move to a rewire firm.
Use **AI for fault-finding** as it improves.
Save **300 a month** and keep the car.
feel: I feel **anxious**, with some control but a deadline.
S3.quote: Five years is long enough to learn old houses, if I stop telling myself new-build will last.
fieldNote: Marco sets himself a **personal deadline** to leave new-build.
He worries for **Kofi**, 45, whose checking job could go too.
He'd delay the **house purchase** about three years.

steps.text: Move to a rewire firm within two years
Use AI tools for fault-finding on jobs
Buy the house with Aisha only after the move

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: The last one is called AGI by 2036. Last one. Full AGI arrives within 10 years, by 2036: AI that can do almost any thinking work a person can do. Robots that can do hands-on work as well as people come about 3 years later, around 2039. It's the same end point, but there's about a decade to prepare, change careers and make plans.

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: Ten years, robots in 2039. That's a whole stretch of career before anything changes.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: If this happened, what would you say about it at work, to friends, or online?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: I'd say there's time to plan, so plan. I'd tell the lads there's no need to panic, but don't sleepwalk.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: And just between us, off the record, what do you really think it means for you?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: I think new-build fades over the decade, slowly. Ten years means I can still buy a house on this estate, but I won't be wiring the next one.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: What would you actually do, starting now and in the first year after it arrives? Be as specific as you can.

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: I'd do my licence and move into rewires and repairs in the next few years. I'd go ahead with buying the two-bed with Aisha. I'd keep saving about 250 and use AI when the lads say it's worth it.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: How does it feel, picturing that?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: Still a bit anxious, because of the per-house pay and the estates slowing. But not scared.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: Why still anxious with ten years?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: Because the estate work could dry up for normal reasons, a slow housing market, before robots ever arrive. Robots just add to it.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: What would make you calm?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: A salaried job with a firm that does repairs. If I got that, I'd sleep fine.

say: I'd say there's **time to plan**, so plan.
I'd tell the lads not to panic, but **don't sleepwalk**.
think: I think **new-build** work fades slowly over the decade.
I could still buy a house here, but I won't be wiring the **next estate**.
do: Move into **rewires and repairs** in a few years.
feel: I feel **a bit anxious** about per-house pay, but not scared.
S4.quote: Ten years means I can still buy a house on this estate, but I won't be wiring the next one.
fieldNote: Marco stays anxious because **per-house pay** is shaky with or without robots.
A **salaried repair job** is what would calm him.
He'd go ahead with the **house purchase** here.

steps.text: Move into rewires and repairs within a few years
Buy the two-bed house with Aisha

closing.speaker: interviewer
closing.text: Of the five pictures, which one worries you most, and what would actually help you if it happened?

closing.speaker: persona
closing.text: AGI by 2028, because a housing estate is the first place robots would go. What would help is a salaried job with a repair firm, and some way to get my licence quicker.

closing.speaker: interviewer
closing.text: Is there anything I didn't ask that I should have?

closing.speaker: persona
closing.text: Maybe ask about pay per house. Being paid per house means every slow week, robot or not, comes straight out of my wages.

headlineQuote: Being paid per house means every slow week, robot or not, comes straight out of my wages.
portrait: Marco is a **27-year-old junior** doing first fix on new-build housing estates.
He's paid **per house**, and saw two crews laid off when sales slowed.
He fears **factory wiring kits** and robots will make estate work easy to replace.
He'd **move to rewires** of old houses, faster the shorter the warning.
biggestWorry: **AGI by 2028**, since a housing estate is the first place robots would go.
whatWouldHelp: A **salaried job** at a repair firm.
